summary.text: R1008 (Krisztina Kiss) has registered, explicit authorship of a single study on incremental Gaussian-mixture online anomaly detection evaluated on a 180-day Modbus/TCP capture, reporting F1 within 0.03 of a retrained baseline, 94% lower retraining cost and sub-120 KB memory. This is a testable direction for no-label, site-specific baselining, but it is not evidence of BACnet coverage, per-site false-alarm performance, or plant-manager-readable explanations, so the proposal is a bounded feasibility study contingent on a data-sharing agreement and on-site validation.

technicalRationale.text: Registered evidence shows incremental Gaussian mixtures maintaining F1 within 0.03 of a periodically retrained static GMM on a single 180-day Modbus/TCP capture, with 94% lower retraining compute, under 120 KB memory per instance, drift detected after a planned reconfiguration, and an operator-acknowledgement-based supervised reset tested.
Only Modbus/TCP is evidenced; BACnet/IP feature engineering and baselining are an untested extension requiring separate evaluation, and R1008's registered fields name no BACnet capability.

The abstract reports no precision/recall split, per-site or per-day false-alarm rate, live alarm counts, or operator-facing explanation of individual alerts, so low false-alarm operability and explainability remain unproven against the company's central failure mode.

cooperationScope.text: Frame the work as a bounded joint feasibility study on the company's archives, starting with Modbus/TCP and treating BACnet/IP as a separate extension with its own feature design, baseline fitting and drift handling, plus an explanation layer translating drift into plain-language flags.

No access or participation is represented as granted.

constraints.text: No labelled malicious traffic exists in the company's archives, so evaluation must rest on baseline consistency, controlled injections and operator review rather than true detection rates.

evidence.excerpt: We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us.

Our ProtoSense module watches Modbus and BACnet traffic and is supposed to flag anything that looks wrong. The problem is that none of our clients has ever given us a packet capture that contains a confirmed attack. A few of them have been running their networks for twenty years with no security monitoring at all, so if they were compromised they would not know. We have plenty of normal traffic — we have collected several terabytes of captures from consenting clients over the past three years — but we have nothing labelled as malicious. We tried building a supervised classifier once, fed it data from public ICS datasets, and it flagged so many false positives in real deployments that clients started switching the alerts off. What we actually need is something that learns what normal looks like on a specific site and raises a flag when behaviour drifts from that baseline. We have the traffic archives, we have the hardware to run inference on-device, and we have one engineer who has been reading about anomaly detection for six months. We need a method that works with no attack examples and that we can explain to a plant manager in plain language.

Incremental Gaussian Mixture Models for Online Anomaly Detection in Continuous ICS Traffic Streams

This paper proposes an incremental variant of Gaussian mixture modelling (iGMM) for online anomaly detection in ICS traffic without the need for periodic full retraining. The algorithm maintains a fixed number of Gaussian components (K = 5 to 20 evaluated) and uses a Bayesian update rule to adjust component means, covariances, and weights with each arriving window of observations. Feature vectors are 32-dimensional, derived from 10-second traffic windows. The method was evaluated on a 180-day Modbus/TCP capture from a district heating control network and compared with a static GMM retrained every 24 hours. The iGMM maintained an F1 score within 0.03 of the periodically retrained model while reducing retraining compute cost by 94%. Concept drift induced by a planned process reconfiguration was detected as a persistent anomaly episode; a supervised reset mechanism based on operator acknowledgement was proposed and tested. Memory footprint per detector instance was under 120 KB.

evidence.excerpt: We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us.

Our ProtoSense module watches Modbus and BACnet traffic and is supposed to flag anything that looks wrong. The problem is that none of our clients has ever given us a packet capture that contains a confirmed attack. A few of them have been running their networks for twenty years with no security monitoring at all, so if they were compromised they would not know. We have plenty of normal traffic — we have collected several terabytes of captures from consenting clients over the past three years — but we have nothing labelled as malicious. We tried building a supervised classifier once, fed it data from public ICS datasets, and it flagged so many false positives in real deployments that clients started switching the alerts off. What we actually need is something that learns what normal looks like on a specific site and raises a flag when behaviour drifts from that baseline. We have the traffic archives, we have the hardware to run inference on-device, and we have one engineer who has been reading about anomaly detection for six months. We need a method that works with no attack examples and that we can explain to a plant manager in plain language.

ArmaturaSec d.o.o. has been building network security hardware in Zrenjanin since 2008. We started by selling simple firewall appliances to regional electricity distributors who needed to segment their control networks from corporate IT. Over fifteen years that focus narrowed: today every product we ship is designed specifically for operational technology environments — the kind of networks that run pumps, switchgear, and assembly lines, not office computers.

Our customers are energy utilities, water treatment operators, and discrete manufacturers in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. They are not looking for cloud dashboards or vendor lock-in; they need a device that sits in a metal cabinet at a substation or pump station, runs for years without attention, and tells someone when something is wrong.

We have 67 people in Zrenjanin. About half write firmware or do hardware bring-up; the rest handle sales, installation, and support. Our head of engineering, Radovan Čičić, joined from a SCADA integrator in 2011 and has led every product generation since. We do not resell other vendors' software. Everything that runs on our appliances — the protocol parsers, the access control engine, the alerting logic — is written and maintained by our own team.

value.bio: Krisztina Kiss received her Dipl.Ing. degree in computer engineering from the University of Novi Sad in 2001 and her PhD in electrical and computer engineering from the same institution in 2008, with a dissertation on statistical traffic profiling in industrial Ethernet networks. She joined the Department of Computing and Control Engineering as an assistant professor in 2009 and was promoted to full professor in 2020. Her research group focuses on unsupervised anomaly detection and one-class classification for industrial control system protocol traffic, using statistical baseline modelling, kernel methods, and lightweight online learning algorithms suited to constrained embedded environments. She teaches courses on network security, operating systems, and industrial communication protocols. The group operates a dedicated ICS testbed equipped with Siemens-compatible PLCs, Modbus/TCP and DNP3 traffic generators, and packet capture infrastructure for long-term dataset collection.
